q: Is Qortal a cryptocurrency?
aliases: is qortal just a crypto coin
a: Qortal is more than a coin. It is an open network that people use to publish websites and apps, chat, hold an identity and trade, running on nodes its own users operate. QORT is the network's native coin: it pays network fees and rewards the minters who keep the chain going. QORT is part of Qortal, but Qortal itself is the infrastructure.

q: What is the difference between Qortal and QORT?
aliases: is qort the same as qortal
a: Qortal is the network: the blockchain, the Qortal Data Network (QDN), the Q-Apps and the people running nodes. QORT is the network's native coin, used for fees, payments and minting rewards. In short, Qortal is the blockchain and QORT is the coin.

q: Is Qortal a fork of Bitcoin or another blockchain?
a: No. Qortal is not a clone or fork of Bitcoin, Ethereum or any other chain. Its code was written from scratch, apart from a few pieces of the old QORA transaction framework. Good ideas from QORA, such as hosting data on the network, were kept but rebuilt in new code.

q: Is Qortal open source?

q: Does Qortal use central servers?
a: No. Qortal runs on nodes: computers running Qortal Core that connect peer to peer, check the blockchain and share QDN data. Most are run by ordinary users. Public nodes exist for easy access, but they are simply nodes that someone else runs, and you can run your own instead.
source: qortal.dev/faq ('Is Qortal decentralized?'); qortal.org (Get Started)

q: What does local-first mean for Qortal?
a: Local-first means the preferred setup is your own Qortal Core node and your own account keys on your device, with no service in the middle. Hub keeps your keys encrypted and signs actions; your local Core checks and shares network data. Hosted access through a public node is offered as an easier first step, but it depends on someone else's machine.
source: qortal.org (About: 'Local before remote'; Technology)

q: What are Qortal's guiding ideas?
a:
qortal.org names four:
Local before remote: your own Core and keys first, hosted access as an easier start.
Protocol before platform: shared rules, signed transactions and names do the work of a central service.

Capability before hype: describe what exists now and mark beta work as beta.

q: Why is Qortal called an alternative internet?
a: Because it offers its own versions of things the usual internet gets from companies: websites and apps hosted on QDN instead of web hosts, registered names instead of domain names, plus messaging, wallets and peer-to-peer trading, all on nodes run by users. It still travels over normal internet connections today.
source: qortal.dev home ('An alternative internet where you fully control your data'); Qortal Core README.md

q: Does Qortal replace my internet provider?
aliases: do I still need an isp for qortal
a: Not today. Your node and apps reach other Qortal peers over your normal internet connection. A mesh network built on Reticulum is Qortal's current development phase and aims to reduce that dependence over time, but it is still evolving and does not replace your provider yet.

q: Is Qortal unhackable?
a: No software is unhackable, and qortal.org says so plainly: spreading the network over many nodes and keeping keys on your own device reduce dependence on any single operator, but they do not make software invulnerable or guarantee it is always available. The part you control is your own safety: keep your seed phrase and backup file private and download Qortal only from official sources.

q: Does Qortal have smart contracts?
a: Yes, in the form of ATs (Automated Transactions): small programs that run on the Qortal blockchain, written in an AT language created by the CIYAM developers. AT accounts have addresses starting with A instead of Q.

q: Why did Qortal launch without an ICO?
a: The founders considered selling coins to investors before launch unethical: it enriches a chosen few, and many ICOs never delivered what they promised. So Qortal started with zero QORT, and every coin since has been minted by people keeping the network running. The trade-off was slow funding; in the early years most developers worked on Qortal alongside day jobs.
source: wiki.qortal.org (Project FAQ: 'Why launch in phases?'; Qortal 101; Founding Team Hardships)

q: Was there an airdrop of QORT?
a: No. Qortal launched with no ICO, no pre-mine and no airdrop. New QORT comes only from block rewards to minters, plus the slow repayment to people who burned legacy QORA before launch. Treat any 'QORT airdrop' that asks for your seed phrase, backup file or a payment as a scam.
source: wiki.qortal.org (Qortal In A Nutshell: 'no ICO, pre-mine, or airdrop'; The QORA Transition)

q: Why is there no cap on the QORT supply?
a: Block rewards are meant never to end, so the network keeps paying the people who keep it running for as long as it exists, instead of relying on high fees. The community wiki adds that Qortal aims to keep fees small and expects the network to outlive its founders. The reward per block shrinks in steps over time, down to a floor.
source: qortal.dev/wiki/minting (Block Rewards: 'meant to be never-ending'); wiki.qortal.org (Qortal 101: No Total Coin Cap)

Q-Apps are ordinary web apps (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) stored on QDN and opened in Hub or GO, which ask you to approve each wallet action. Qortal had no ICO or pre-mine, uses minting instead of staking, and its smart contracts are ATs, used mainly for trades and crowdfunding.

q: Why was QORA rebuilt as Qortal?
a: QORA was a blockchain launched in 2014 with ideas such as hosting data on the network. But it used proof of stake, which lets money buy power, and it had a bloated chain, an over-inflated coin supply and a tangled codebase; its founding team eventually abandoned it. In 2016 crowetic gathered a development group that offered the QORA community a complete rebuild: keep the good ideas, fix the flaws and remove proof of stake entirely.

q: What was in Qortal's Genesis block?
a: The Genesis block (29 June 2020, 17:00 UTC) set the network up rather than handing out coins. It created QORT with a quantity of zero, recorded the legacy QORA that holders had burned as unspendable marker assets, set starting levels 1 to 5 for the first minters, such as QORA forgers, flagged 19 founder accounts and created the developer group. Every QORT in existence came from block rewards after that.

q: How many QORT existed at Genesis?

Since block 2,206,300 that starting credit no longer counts towards an account's level: levels now come only from blocks actually minted on Qortal (minus any penalties).

q: How is a Qortal address made?
aliases: how is a qortal address created
where does my qortal address come from
a: Your address is calculated from your account's public key: the key is hashed (SHA-256, then RIPEMD-160), a version byte goes in front, and a short checksum goes at the end. The result is written in Base58, giving 34 characters that start with Q. Because it comes from your key, you cannot choose or change your address; a registered name is the readable alternative.
source: Qortal Core source (crypto/Crypto.java toAddress, ADDRESS_VERSION 58)

q: How many characters are in a Qortal address?
aliases: is my qortal address too short
a: A Qortal account address is 34 characters long and starts with Q. It uses Base58, a set of letters and digits that leaves out easily confused characters such as 0, O, I and l. If what you copied has more or fewer than 34 characters, part of the address is missing or extra.
source: Qortal Core source (utils/Base58.java alphabet; transform/Transformer.java ADDRESS_LENGTH 25 bytes; genesis addresses in blockchain.json are all 34 characters)

q: Does a Qortal address have a checksum?
aliases: one wrong letter in qortal address
a: Yes. The end of every Qortal address is a checksum calculated from the rest, so a mistyped or partly copied address almost always shows as invalid instead of pointing at someone else. It cannot catch a valid address that belongs to the wrong person, so check the whole address before you send: on-chain payments cannot be reversed.
source: Qortal Core source (crypto/Crypto.java toAddress checksum, areValidTypedAddressBytes)

q: Can I choose my own Qortal address?
a: No. Your address is calculated from your account's key, so it is fixed and you cannot pick or change it. What you can choose is a registered name, which people can use instead of your address, for example to send you QORT or a Q-Mail. A different address means a different, new account.
source: Qortal Core source (crypto/Crypto.java toAddress); Welcome-to-Qortal src/pages/GettingStarted.jsx (receiving QORT by name)

q: Is my Qortal address case-sensitive?
aliases: qortal address upper and lower case
a: Yes. Addresses use Base58, where capital and small letters are different characters, so changing the case breaks the address and its checksum fails. Copy and paste addresses, or scan a payment QR code where the app offers one, rather than retyping them.
source: Qortal Core source (utils/Base58.java alphabet; crypto/Crypto.java checksum)

q: What is a public key on Qortal?
aliases: what is my public key used for
a: Your public key is the public half of your account's key pair, an Ed25519 key usually shown as about 44 characters. The network uses it to check that a transaction really was signed by your account, and apps use it to encrypt messages and data that only you can open. Your address is calculated from it. It is safe to share; your seed phrase and private key are not.

q: What is the difference between my address and my public key?
aliases: seed phrase public key address difference
difference between address and public key
a: Your seed phrase is the master secret that generates your account; never share it. Your public key comes from it and proves you own the account without revealing the secret, and apps use it to encrypt things for you. Your address is a shorter identifier calculated from the public key, used for payments and on-chain references. Think of them as root password, identity and account number.

q: Is it safe to share my Qortal address?
aliases: can I give out my qortal address

Its public key is recorded on-chain the first time the account makes an outgoing transaction, such as a payment, a name registration or joining a group; the community wiki calls this activating the account. Until then, things that need your public key, such as others sending you encrypted messages, may not work.

a: In two ways. Your balances, names and transactions are on the Qortal blockchain, which the network's nodes keep copies of. q: Why would a Qortal transaction cost more than 0.01 QORT?
aliases: why is my qortal fee higher
a: The 0.01 QORT fee is a unit fee: Core charges one unit for each started 1,024 bytes of transaction data. Most transactions, such as payments and votes, fit in one unit and cost 0.01 QORT; QDN publishes usually do too, because the file itself stays off-chain. A transaction carrying more data, such as a long poll description, pays a unit per 1,024 bytes. Registering a name has its own fee of 1.25 QORT.

q: What is a block in the Qortal blockchain?

Each block points back to the one before it, so together they form a permanent, ordered record, and every node checks each block against the rules before accepting it. A block also records the online minters who took part in producing it.

Your node's height shows how far it has synced, and when it matches the network's, your node is up to date. Heights only go up, about one per minute.

q: What is a re-org on Qortal?
a: Sometimes parts of the network briefly build on different blocks. Each node compares the competing chains and switches to the one with more chain weight, which comes mostly from how many online minters are counted in its blocks. Blocks dropped this way are orphaned, and their transactions go back to waiting for a block. It usually settles within a couple of blocks and is normal.
source: wiki.qortal.org (How Qortal's Consensus Works: 're-org ... within a couple of blocks'); Qortal Core source (block/Block.java calcBlockWeight, orphanTransactionsFromBlock)

q: How do Qortal nodes agree on the blockchain?
aliases: which chain does my node follow
how does the qortal network agree
a: Every node checks each block and transaction against the same rules, such as valid signatures, enough balance for fees and correct rewards, and rejects anything that breaks them. When chains compete, nodes follow the one with the most weight, mainly the one whose blocks count the most online minters. Who signs each block comes from a verifiable draw based on minters' keys, so nobody can buy their way into producing blocks.
source: wiki.qortal.org (How Qortal's Consensus Works); Qortal Core source (block/Block.java calcKeyDistance, calcBlockWeight, calcChainWeight)

q: Why do Qortal block times vary?
a: Each block must be stamped between 30 and 90 seconds after the one before, with 60 seconds as the target. Where it lands in that window depends on how close the signer's key is to that block's ideal key and on the signer's level, so the gap changes from block to block. The community wiki puts the long-run average at around 65 seconds.
source: Qortal Core source (blockchain.json blockTimingsByHeight target 60000, deviation 30000; block/Block.java calcTimestamp); wiki.qortal.org (How Qortal's Consensus Works)

q: What counts as a transaction on Qortal?
a: A transaction is a signed instruction from an account that the network records in a block: a payment, a name registration, a QDN publish, joining a group, creating or voting in a poll, a trade contract and more. Qortal Core defines 41 transaction types. Each one is signed with the sender's key, checked by every node, and usually costs a small fee.
source: Qortal Core source (transaction/Transaction.java TransactionType enum); wiki.qortal.org (Qortal Glossary: Ledger)

q: What does on-chain mean?
aliases: is it stored on the qortal blockchain
a: On-chain means recorded in the Qortal blockchain itself, in blocks every node keeps and checks: payments, names, group memberships, polls and the records of QDN publishes. Off-chain means stored elsewhere, like the files of a QDN website, which live on the nodes that host them while an on-chain hash proves what was published and by which name.
source: wiki.qortal.org (Qortal Glossary: On-Chain); qortal.org (Technology: Qortal Data Network)

q: What does peer-to-peer mean?
a: Peer-to-peer (P2P) means computers deal with each other directly, with no central server in the middle. On Qortal, nodes connect to other nodes, their peers, to share blocks, transactions and QDN data; trades happen between the two traders' own wallets; and Reticulum Q-Chat goes from device to device.

q: What does decentralised mean?
a: Decentralised means no single company, server or person runs the system. On Qortal, many independently run nodes keep copies of the blockchain and QDN data, check each other's work, and the network keeps going if any of them disappear. No one can switch it off or change the rules on their own.

q: What is a poll on Qortal?

People vote with VOTE_ON_POLL transactions, each with the normal small fee. Apps build on polls: Q-Mintership attaches one to each nomination, and Hub uses polls for Q-App star ratings.

q: What is a blockchain?
a: A blockchain is a shared record, or ledger, kept by many computers called nodes. New transactions are grouped into blocks; each block is checked by the nodes and linked to the one before, so past entries cannot be quietly changed. Qortal's blockchain records payments, names, groups, polls and QDN publish records, and minters add a new block about once a minute.

q: What is a hash, and why does Qortal use them?

QDN records a hash of each publish on-chain, so anyone can check that the copy they downloaded is exactly what was published, and your address is made by hashing your public key.
